claims.text: Enhanced free-energy integration using metadynamics or umbrella sampling in multicomponent molecular dynamics can accurately predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting-volume change, and liquid thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The proposed enhanced-sampling approach can evaluate these properties efficiently across diverse HEA compositions.
The target HEAs are multicomponent solid solutions near their melting points.
Compositional variability gives HEAs complex free-energy landscapes near melting.
A metadynamics- or umbrella-sampling-based MD scheme can sample the HEA free-energy landscape and compute solid–liquid transition thermodynamics.
The free-energy landscape governs the solid–liquid phase transition.
Relevant features of this landscape include saddle points, latent-heat contributions, and structural rearrangements at the solid–liquid interface.
Biasing the system evolution with enhanced sampling reduces the difficulty of crossing large free-energy barriers.
Reducing barrier-crossing difficulty enables efficient sampling of the complete melting process.
Atomistic simulation data can be integrated into macroscopic thermodynamic parameters.
The resulting quantitative predictions can be compared directly with calorimetric and dilatometric measurements.
Predicted melting temperatures and fusion enthalpies and entropies will agree with experiment within 5–10%.
Melting-volume changes and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties will be predicted with similar precision.
The proposed approach will be computationally more efficient than traditional ab initio or full CALPHAD methods.
Traditional calorimetric and dilatometric measurements are too labor-intensive to cover HEA compositional complexity effectively.
Ab initio molecular-dynamics simulations are too computationally expensive to cover HEA compositional complexity effectively.
The approach may be unreliable for HEAs without well-validated interatomic potentials.
Prohibitively high barriers or extremely rugged free-energy surfaces may prevent convergence within realistic simulation times.
The method is most suitable for alloy systems with documented phase equilibria and thermodynamic datasets.

The approach is to be considered falsified if predictions for at least three distinct HEA compositions deviate by more than 10% from experiment for melting temperature, fusion enthalpy or entropy, or melting-volume change.
